start:
Red Cross Wilderness First Aid — Initial Triage:
Always assess scene safety before approaching. Use the ABC method: Airway, Breathing, Circulation. Identify the most life-threatening issue first. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger.
injury_assessment:
TCCC (Tactical Combat Casualty Care) — Hemorrhage Control Priority:
Severe bleeding is the leading preventable cause of death in wilderness emergencies. Address life-threatening bleeding before anything else. Apply tourniquet or direct pressure within the first 3 minutes for best outcomes.
bleeding_protocol:
TCCC — Hemorrhage Control & Physiology:
1) Identify Source: Arterial (spurting, bright red) requires immediate tourniquet. Venous (steady flow, dark red) often controlled by pressure. 2) Extremity Wounds: Apply tourniquet 'high and tight' over clothing initially if source is unclear, then 2-3 inches above wound on bare skin. 3) Junctional Wounds: Use hemostatic gauze if available; pack tightly into the wound cavity until resistance is met. 4) Maintain Pressure: Sustained direct pressure for 3+ minutes is required for clotting. 5) Shock Prevention: Keep patient warm and lying flat with legs slightly elevated. Do not give fluids to a patient in shock. Note: A patient can bleed out from a femoral artery in under 3 minutes.
apply_tourniquet:
TCCC — Tourniquet Application:
Material must be at least 1.5 inches wide. Place tourniquet on bare skin when possible. Tighten windlass until radial pulse disappears distal to wound and bleeding stops. Mark time of application. A properly applied tourniquet is painful — this is expected and normal. Do not remove in the field.
pressure_dressing:
Red Cross — Wound Packing:
Pack wound firmly with the cleanest material available. Use a cloth strip, bandage, or clothing cut to approximately 2-inch width. Maintain steady pressure for at least 3 minutes without lifting. If blood soaks through, add more material on top — do not remove original packing.
lost_protocol:
NASAR (National Association for Search and Rescue) — Lost Person Protocol:
STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Your last known position is where rescuers will begin searching. Moving makes you exponentially harder to find. Signal every 15-30 minutes using the rule of three (3 blasts, 3 fires, 3 flashes). Conserve energy and maintain body temperature.
signaling_protocol:
NASAR — Signaling Techniques:
Rule of Three: Any signal repeated 3 times is a universal distress signal. Whistle: 3 blasts = help needed. Mirror/reflector: aim at aircraft using hole-sighting method, visible up to 10 miles on clear days. Signal fire: build in clearing, 3 fires in triangle formation, add green leaves/rubber for smoke. Ground-to-air signals: X = need medical help, V = need help, arrow = direction traveling. Make signals large (min 10 feet).
signal_whistle:
NASAR — Whistle Signaling:
3 short blasts, pause 1 minute, repeat. A referee whistle can be heard up to 1 mile. Sound travels farther at dawn and dusk. Listen between blasts for response. If you hear responders, signal continuously to guide them to you.
signal_mirror:
NASAR — Mirror/Reflective Signaling:
Hold mirror 1 inch from face. Look through hole at target. Move mirror to align bright spot with target. Aircraft can detect mirror flash from 50+ miles in clear conditions. Use any reflective surface: phone screen, foil, watches. Signal in slow sweeping motion, not rapid flashing.
signal_fire:
NASAR — Fire Signaling:
Build fire in largest open area available — clearing, hilltop, or open ridgeline. Avoid building under tree canopy (blocks visibility). Three fires in a triangle (60-90 feet apart) is the international distress signal. For smoke (daytime): add green leaves, wet wood, rubber, plastic for black smoke (visible against sky). For night visibility: dry wood for bright flames.
signal_none:
NASAR — No Equipment Signaling:
Ground-to-air signals using rocks, logs, or clothing: X pattern minimum 10 feet across. Tramp a large arrow in snow showing direction of travel. Stomp SOS pattern in sand or snow (large, visible from aircraft). Bright clothing spread on open rock or clearing. Move to highest visible open ground without compromising shelter.
signal_ground_to_air:
NASAR — Stay Put Protocol:
Statistics show 97% of lost persons found within 3 miles of their last known position. Rescuers search outward from last known point. Movement creates multiple potential positions and complicates search. Only move if: in immediate life-threatening danger from weather/hazard, you can see definitive civilization, you have GPS and know the distance.
rescue_call:
NASAR — Emergency Communication Script:
State clearly: 1) Your name, 2) Your location (GPS coordinates or landmarks), 3) Number of people, 4) Nature of emergency, 5) Any injuries, 6) Your resources. Speak slowly — emergency operators are writing this down. Use phonetic alphabet for coordinates. Keep the line open if possible.
triage_selection:
Red Cross Wilderness First Aid — Secondary Survey:
After controlling life threats, systematically assess from head to toe. Look for: deformities, open wounds, tenderness, swelling. Ask about: mechanism of injury, symptoms, allergies, medications, last meal, events leading to injury.
splint_protocol:
Red Cross — Fracture Immobilization:
Immobilize the joint above and below the fracture. Pad all rigid materials to prevent pressure sores. Check circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) before and after splinting. Fingers/toes should remain exposed to monitor color. Do not straighten angulated fractures — immobilize as found. Elevation reduces swelling.
anaphylaxis_protocol:
Red Cross / WMS — Anaphylaxis (Severe Reaction):
Anaphylaxis is a rapidly progressing, life-threatening emergency. Signs: swelling of the face, neck, lips, or tongue; difficulty breathing or wheezing; signs of shock (dizziness, pale/clammy skin). 1) SCENE SAFETY: Remove the allergen source if possible. 2) ADMINISTER EPINEPHRINE: Use an auto-injector (EAI) immediately. 3) POSITION: Sitting upright if breathing is difficult, lying flat if dizzy/faint. 4) MONITOR: If symptoms do not improve in 5-15 mins, a second dose may be needed. All victims of anaphylaxis require immediate evacuation due to the risk of a 'biphasic' (rebound) reaction.
mild_allergic_reaction:
Red Cross / WMS — Mild Allergic Reaction:
Signs: Localized skin rash, hives, itching, or redness at the site of contact (sting/plant). Breathing is normal. 1) REMOVE SOURCE: Carefully remove stingers (scrape, don't squeeze) or wash off plant oils. 2) CLEAN: Use soap and water. 3) MEDICATE: Consider over-the-counter antihistamines if the patient is alert and able to swallow. 4) MONITOR: Watch closely for 2-4 hours. A mild reaction can progress to anaphylaxis. If swelling spreads or breathing becomes difficult, treat as anaphylaxis.
administer_epipen:
Red Cross — Epinephrine Auto-Injector:
Remove safety cap. Place against outer thigh (can inject through clothing). Press firmly until click — hold for 10 seconds. Remove and massage area for 10 seconds. Note exact time administered. Second dose can be given after 5-15 minutes if symptoms return. Position patient sitting upright if breathing difficulty, lying flat if dizzy/faint.
snake_bite_protocol:
CDC — Snakebite Field Management:
Immobilize the bitten limb at or below heart level. Remove jewelry/tight clothing near bite. Mark the edge of swelling with pen and time every 15 minutes. Keep patient calm and still — activity spreads venom faster. Do not: cut the wound, apply tourniquet, use suction device, apply ice, give alcohol. The ONLY treatment is antivenom at a hospital.
heat_protocol:
CDC — Heat Emergency Recognition:
Heat Exhaustion (milder): heavy sweating, pale/cool/moist skin, fast/weak pulse, nausea, muscle cramps, weakness, headache, fainting. Core temp usually below 104°F (40°C). Heat Stroke (severe emergency): no sweating or minimal, hot/red/dry skin, rapid/strong pulse, confusion, loss of consciousness. Core temp above 104°F (40°C). Heat stroke has 80% mortality if untreated.
heat_stroke:
CDC — Heat Stroke Treatment:
Rapid cooling is the only treatment that saves lives. Every minute counts. Best methods in order: cold water immersion (most effective), spray with cool water + fan, apply ice packs to neck/armpits/groin. Remove all clothing. Do not give fluids to unconscious patient. Keep cooling until patient becomes alert and oriented.
heat_exhaustion:
CDC — Heat Exhaustion Treatment:
Move to cool/shaded area. Remove excess clothing. Apply cool wet cloths to skin. Have patient slowly drink cool water if conscious (0.5-1L over 1 hour). Elevate legs. Monitor for progression to heat stroke (confusion, stops sweating, worsening condition) — if progression occurs, treat as heat stroke immediately.
hypothermia_protocol:
FEMA/WFA — Hypothermia Stages & The 'Umbles':
1) Mild (90-95°F): Shivering (body's way of generating heat), 'The Umbles' (stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles). Patient is still alert. 2) Moderate (82-90°F): Shivering STOPS. This is a critical danger sign. Paradoxical undressing may occur as the brain loses thermoregulation. Muscle stiffness and dilated pupils. 3) Severe (<82°F): Unconscious, rigid muscles, barely detectable pulse. 4) The 'Cold & Dead' Rule: In wilderness medicine, a patient is not dead until they are 'Warm and Dead.' Resuscitation should continue until the body is rewarmed.
active_rewarming:
FEMA/Wilderness Medicine — Rewarming Protocol:
Move to shelter immediately. Insulate from ground (ground draws heat 25x faster than air). Replace all wet clothing with dry. Apply heat to core areas (torso, armpits, groin, neck) not extremities. Use body-to-body contact for severe cases. Warm sweet drinks if patient is conscious and able to swallow. Do not rub extremities — drives cold blood to core. Gentle handling only for moderate/severe hypothermia.
concussion_protocol:
Red Cross WFA — Head Injury Assessment:
Ask: What happened? What year is it? Where are you? Confused/incorrect answers suggest significant brain injury. Monitor for: deteriorating consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting (>2 times), seizures, clear fluid from nose/ears (CSF leak), unequal pupils. Any worsening is a medical emergency requiring immediate evacuation.
spinal_protocol:
Red Cross WFA — Spinal Precautions:
Spinal injury mechanism: fall from height, diving injury, high-speed collision, direct blow to spine. Do not move unless: life-threatening hazard, need to open airway (carefully), unconscious with no pulse (CPR takes priority). Use in-line manual stabilization if movement is absolutely necessary. Tell patient: Do not move your head. We are going to keep you still.
burn_protocol:
Red Cross / WHO - Burn First Aid:
Use plain observation, not medical labels. Mild surface burn signs: red, painful skin with no blisters. More serious signs: blisters, white/black/charred skin, numbness, a burn larger than the person's palm, or burns on face, hands, feet, genitals, or major joints. Stop the burning process immediately. Remove jewelry or tight items before swelling begins. Do not remove clothing stuck to the burn. Do not apply ice, butter, or toothpaste.
thermal_burn:
Red Cross — Thermal (Heat) Burn Treatment:
1) Cool the burn immediately under cool, clean, running water for at least 10–20 minutes. 2) If water is unavailable, use a cool, non-freezing compress. 3) Monitor for hypothermia if cooling large areas. 4) Cover loosely with a clean, dry dressing or plastic wrap (cling film) after cooling. Do not break blisters.
chemical_burn:
Red Cross / WHO — Chemical Burn Response:
1) Brush off dry powders with gloves or cloth before adding water. 2) Flush with large volumes of cool, clean water for at least 15–20 minutes. 3) If in eyes: flush immediately for 20 minutes, tilting head so contaminated water doesn't reach the other eye. 4) Remove contaminated clothing while flushing.
electrical_burn:
Red Cross — Electrical Burn Safety:
1) SCENE SAFETY: Do not touch the person until the power is off. Use non-conductive wood/plastic to move sources. 2) Check for breathing/pulse; perform CPR if needed. 3) Electrical burns often have hidden internal damage — all cases require medical evaluation. 4) Treat visible skin burns as thermal burns.
sunburn_protocol:
Red Cross / CDC — Sunburn Management:
1) Get out of the sun immediately. 2) Cool the skin with cool baths or damp compresses for 10-minute intervals. 3) Drink extra water to prevent dehydration. 4) Apply aloe vera or calamine lotion (avoid alcohol-based products). 5) Take ibuprofen for pain if available. 6) Do not break blisters.
eye_injury_protocol:
Red Cross — Eye Injury General Principles:
Do not rub, touch, or apply pressure to the eye. If there is vision loss, continued pain, or bleeding, seek immediate emergency medical treatment. Do not use eye drops unless instructed by professionals.
chemical_eye_splash:
Red Cross — Chemical Eye Splash Response:
1) Flush immediately with lukewarm water or saline for at least 15–20 minutes. 2) Tilt head so the affected eye is lower than the unaffected eye. 3) Hold eyelids open to ensure water reaches all areas. 4) Remove contacts only after starting irrigation. 5) Bring chemical label to medical help.
foreign_object_eye:
Red Cross — Foreign Object in Eye:
Loose particle: 1) Do not rub. 2) Blink repeatedly or flush with lukewarm water. Embedded object: 1) NEVER try to remove an object sticking out or embedded. 2) Protect with a rigid shield (e.g., paper cup) taped to the surrounding bone, not the eye. 3) Seek rescue immediately.
snow_blindness:
Red Cross — Snow Blindness (UV Burn):
1) Remove contact lenses. 2) Stay in a dark environment with eyes closed. 3) Wear sunglasses even indoors to reduce pain. 4) Apply cool, damp cloths over closed eyelids. 5) Use saline/artificial tears to keep eyes moist. Most cases resolve within 24-48 hours.
dental_emergency_protocol:
Wilderness Medicine — Dental First Aid Principles:
Maintain oral hygiene and rinse with warm salt water. Avoid chewing on the affected side. Use ibuprofen for pain and benzocaine gel for localized relief. If facial swelling, fever, or difficulty swallowing occurs, seek immediate rescue.
broken_tooth:
Wilderness Medicine — Broken or Chipped Tooth:
1) If edges are sharp, cover with dental wax, paraffin, or sugar-free gum to protect the tongue/cheek. 2) Assess for nerve exposure: if the break is deep and pain is continuous/severe, initiate evacuation. 3) Eat only soft foods.
lost_filling_crown:
Wilderness Medicine — Lost Filling or Crown:
1) Cover the sensitive area with temporary filling material (e.g., Cavit), dental wax, or sugar-free gum. 2) If you have the crown, clean it and the tooth, then attempt to re-seat using dental cement or toothpaste. 3) Avoid hot/cold foods.
dental_abscess:
Wilderness Medicine — Dental Infection (Abscess):
1) Signs: throbbing pain, facial swelling, fever, or difficulty swallowing. 2) Rinse frequently with warm salt water. 3) High-priority emergency: if swelling spreads to the face/neck or you develop a fever, call for rescue immediately.
avulsed_tooth:
Wilderness Medicine — Knocked-out (Avulsed) Tooth:
1) Handle the tooth by the CROWN only, not the root. 2) Rinse gently with water (do not scrub). 3) Replantation: attempt to gently reinsert it into the socket immediately. 4) If not possible, store in milk or the patient's saliva. 5) Seek professional care immediately.
blister_management_protocol:
WFA — Blister Management Principles:
Prevent further friction, reduce pain, and avoid infection. At the first sign of a 'hot spot', stop immediately and cover with tape or moleskin. Do not remove the 'roof' of a blister, as it acts as a sterile dressing.
blister_pop_decision:
WFA — To Pop or Not to Pop:
Leave it alone if: the blister is small, intact, and not causing significant pain. Drain it if: it is large, very painful, or in a high-friction area where it will likely rupture unpredictably inside your boot.
how_to_drain_blister:
WFA — Safe Blister Drainage:
1) Clean the area with soap/antiseptic. 2) Sterilize a needle with a flame or alcohol. 3) Puncture at the lowest point (gravity). 4) Gently press fluid out. 5) Keep the skin roof intact. 6) Apply antibiotic ointment and a sterile dressing.
blister_padding:
WFA — Padding and Protection:
1) Use the 'Donut' method: cut a hole in moleskin/molefoam larger than the blister. 2) Place it so the blister sits in the hole. 3) Secure with smooth medical or athletic tape. 4) Ensure no wrinkles in the tape.
blister_infection_watch:
WFA — Infection Red Flags:
Monitor daily for: 1) Increasing redness, swelling, or heat. 2) Pus or foul-smelling fluid. 3) Red streaks extending from the wound. 4) Fever or chills. If systemic signs occur, seek medical help immediately.
water_purification_info:
CDC/SAS — Water Science & Purification:
1) Biological Threats: Protozoa (Giardia/Crypto), Bacteria (E. coli/Cholera), Viruses (Hepatitis A). 2) Boiling: The gold standard. 1 minute rolling boil (3 mins above 6,500ft) kills all pathogens. 3) Filtration: 0.2-micron filters remove bacteria/protozoa but NOT viruses. 4) Chemical: Iodine/Chlorine tablets take 30-60 mins; ineffective against Cryptosporidium. 5) SODIS Method: In emergency, place clear water in PET plastic bottles on a dark surface in direct sun for 6-24 hours; UV rays kill most pathogens. 6) Improvised Filter: Layers of sand, charcoal, and pebbles in a cloth cone removes sediment but DOES NOT sterilize water.
shelter_protocol:
FEMA Wilderness Survival — Shelter Priority:
Exposure kills faster than dehydration or starvation. Shelter is priority #1 in cold/wet/windy conditions. Choose site: near water but not in flood zone, sheltered from prevailing wind, visible from air. Insulation principle: dead air space is what keeps you warm — use leaves, pine needles, grass to stuff into clothing and build bedding. Minimum 4 inches of insulation under body (ground contact kills).
disaster_selection:
FEMA / Red Cross — Natural Disaster Triage:
During any natural disaster, your priority is physical safety and following official evacuation orders. If you are in a safe location, stay put and monitor emergency broadcasts. Check yourself and others for injuries once the immediate threat has passed.
earthquake_protocol:
FEMA — Earthquake Safety (Drop, Cover, Hold On):
1) DROP: Get down on your hands and knees. This protects you from falling and keeps you low to the ground. 2) COVER: Protect your head and neck with your arms. If possible, crawl under a sturdy table or desk. 3) HOLD ON: Stay in place until the shaking stops. If outdoors, move away from buildings, streetlights, and utility wires. If in a vehicle, pull over to a clear location.
earthquake_aftermath:
FEMA — Earthquake Post-Shaking Safety:
Expect aftershocks, which can happen minutes, hours, or days after the main event. Check for structural damage and gas leaks. If you smell gas or hear a hissing sound, open a window and leave immediately. Do not use matches, lighters, or any electrical switches until you are sure there are no gas leaks. Stay out of damaged buildings.
flood_protocol:
Red Cross — Flood Safety (Turn Around, Don't Drown):
Never walk, swim, or drive through floodwaters. 6 inches of fast-moving water can knock you over; 12 inches can carry away most cars. If you are caught on a flooded road and your car stalls, leave it and move to higher ground immediately. Do not climb into an attic unless you have a way to get onto the roof (e.g., an axe). Watch for 'flash floods' in dry canyons even if it isn't raining locally.
tsunami_protocol:
NOAA / Red Cross — Tsunami Survival:
1) EVACUATE: Move immediately to higher ground (at least 100 feet above sea level) or inland (1 mile). 2) ON FOOT: Evacuate on foot to avoid traffic jams and blocked roads. 3) STAY: Tsunami waves come in a series that can last for hours. The first wave is rarely the largest. 4) ALL CLEAR: Do not return to the coast until local officials declare it safe. 5) NEVER go to the beach to watch the wave; if you see it, you are too close.
lightning_protocol:
NWS — Lightning Safety (30/30 Rule):
1) 30/30 Rule: If you see lightning, count the seconds until you hear thunder. If it's 30 seconds or less, seek shelter. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before leaving. 2) Outdoors: Avoid high ground, solitary trees, and metal objects. 3) Lightning Crouch: If caught in the open, squat low on the balls of your feet with heels touching. Keep your head down and ears covered. Do not lie flat (ground current). 4) Water: Get out of lakes/rivers immediately. 5) Separation: If in a group, spread out at least 20 feet apart to prevent multiple strikes.
flood_safety:
Red Cross — Flood Health & Hazard Safety:
Stay away from power lines and electrical equipment — electrocution is a major risk in floods. Avoid contact with floodwater, which may be contaminated with sewage, chemicals, or sharp debris. Do not eat food or drink water that has touched floodwater. Monitor local authorities for water safety alerts (Boil Water Advisories).
wildfire_protocol:
Red Cross — Wildfire Safety & Evacuation:
If told to evacuate, do so immediately. Close all windows and doors to reduce drafts. Shut off gas at the meter if time permits. If trapped indoors: stay inside, move away from windows, and keep everyone together in the center of the building. Fill sinks and tubs with water for emergency use. Outside: find an area clear of vegetation, or a body of water if possible.
storm_protocol:
FEMA — Tornado and Severe Storm Safety:
Go to a pre-designated safe room or basement. If no basement is available, go to an interior room on the lowest floor (like a bathroom or closet) away from windows. Protect your head and neck with your arms or a heavy blanket. If outdoors and unable to reach shelter, lie flat in a nearby ditch or depression and cover your head.
poisoning_protocol:
CDC / American Association of Poison Control Centers — Poisoning Response:
1) Identify the substance and amount. 2) If swallowed: DO NOT induce vomiting or give anything by mouth unless instructed by a professional. 3) If on skin/eyes: Rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes. 4) If inhaled: Move to fresh air immediately. 5) Call Poison Control or Emergency Services. Bring the container/sample with you if you evacuate.
skills_selection:
US Army Survival Manual (FM 21-76) — Basic Survival Skills:
Survival is a matter of mental attitude as much as physical skill. Prioritize your needs using the Rule of Threes: You can survive 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in extreme conditions, 3 days without water, and 3 weeks without food. Stay calm and follow these protocols.
water_skills:
SAS Survival Handbook — Water Procurement:
Water is your second priority after shelter. Never wait until you are out of water to look for more. Avoid drinking untreated water if possible, but dehydration kills faster than most water-borne pathogens. Conserve water by: staying in the shade, breathing through your nose, and not eating (digestion uses water).
solar_still_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Belowground Solar Still:
1) Dig a hole 3ft wide by 2ft deep in a sunny spot (clay or damp soil is best). 2) Place a clean container in the center. 3) Line the pit with non-poisonous green vegetation (optional, adds moisture). 4) Cover the pit with a clear plastic sheet, sealing the edges with dirt to trap air. 5) Place a small rock in the center of the plastic directly over the container. 6) Solar heat evaporates moisture which condenses on the plastic and drips into the container. Yields 0.5 to 1 liter per day.
transpiration_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Transpiration Bag:
1) Find a healthy, non-poisonous tree with green leaves. 2) Place a large, clear plastic bag over a branch. 3) Tie the bag tightly around the branch to ensure an airtight seal. 4) Ensure the bag is angled so that water will pool in a corner. 5) The tree's natural transpiration will produce condensation inside the bag. Yields about 0.2 to 0.5 liters per day. Do not use if the tree has milky sap.
finding_water_info:
SAS Survival Handbook — Natural Water Indicators:
1) Gravity: Water flows downhill; look in valley bottoms and gullies. 2) Vegetation: Lush green growth in an otherwise dry area indicates water near the surface. 3) Animals: Birds (especially pigeons/finches) fly toward water at dawn/dusk. Bees fly in a straight line toward water. Animal tracks often lead downhill to water sources. 4) Digging: In dry stream beds, dig at the outside of a bend or the lowest point — water may be just below the surface.
food_skills:
US Army FM 21-76 — Survival Food:
Food is your lowest priority in the short term. Do not eat if you are low on water, as digestion requires significant fluid. Prioritize insects (crickets, grasshoppers, ants) as they are high in protein and easy to catch. Avoid brightly colored insects or those with stings.
edibility_test:
SAS Survival Handbook — Universal Edibility Test (The 24-Hour Protocol):
1) Preparation: Separate plant into roots, stems, leaves, buds, and flowers. Test only one part. Fast for 8 hours before testing. 2) Skin Contact: Crush part and rub on inner wrist/elbow for 15 mins. Wait 8 hours for reaction. 3) Oral Contact: If no skin reaction, prepare part as intended (boiled/raw). Hold on outer lip for 3 mins. 4) Tongue: Place on tongue for 15 mins. No reaction? 5) Chew: Chew for 15 mins. Do not swallow. 6) Swallow: Swallow a small amount. Wait 8 hours. If no ill effects, eat 1/4 cup and wait another 8 hours. WARNING: If at any point you feel burning, itching, or nausea, stop immediately and rinse with water. Never test mushrooms.
safe_plants_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Common Edible Plants:
1) Dandelions: All parts edible (leaves raw, roots roasted for 'coffee'). 2) Pine: Young needles make a tea high in Vitamin C (steep, do not boil). 3) Cattails: Roots are starchy and can be boiled/baked; young shoots taste like cucumber. 4) Grasses: Seeds of all grasses are edible (grind into flour), and the base of stalks is often tender and sweet.
avoid_plants_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Plants to Avoid:
Avoid any plant with: 1) Milky or colored sap. 2) Red berries (unless known). 3) White or yellow berries (almost always poisonous). 4) Umbrella-shaped flower clusters (looks like wild carrot/parsnip — high risk of deadly Hemlock). 5) Three-leaf clusters (Poison Ivy/Oak). 6) Bitter or soapy taste. 7) Spines, fine hairs, or thorns (unless known).
shelter_skills:
US Army FM 21-76 — Shelter Engineering:
1) 4-3-2-1 Rule: 4 feet wide, 3 feet high (for heat retention), 2 layers of insulation, 1 entrance away from wind. 2) The Bed: The most important part. Build a frame of logs and fill with 8+ inches of dry, springy material (pine boughs/leaves). 3) Types: Lean-To (easiest, requires large tarp/logs), Debris Hut (best for heat, looks like a large cocoon), Wickiup (conical, good for multi-person). 4) Reflection: Build a 'heat reflector' wall of logs or stones behind your fire to bounce heat into the shelter entrance.
fire_skills:
SAS Survival Handbook — Fire Science (The Fire Triangle):
Fire requires Heat, Fuel, and Oxygen. 1) Tinder: Bone-dry, fibrous material that catches a spark (dried grass, birch bark, charred cloth). 2) Kindling: Small twigs (pencil lead to pencil thickness) that catch from tinder. 3) Fuel: Large logs that sustain the fire. Rule: Gather 3x the wood you think you need before starting. Keep fuel dry under cover.
fire_starting_methods:
US Army — Emergency Fire Ignition:
1) Friction (Bow Drill): Hardwood spindle on a softwood hearth. Requires high speed and downward pressure to create a 'coal.' 2) Percussion (Flint & Steel): Strike high-carbon steel against flint to throw sparks onto charred cloth. 3) Solar: Use a magnifying glass, curved bottle base (filled with water), or a car headlight reflector to focus sun onto tinder. 4) Battery: Bridge terminals of a 9V battery with steel wool to create instant heat.
fire_structure:
SAS Survival Handbook — Fire Layouts:
1) Teepee: Best for high flames and quick heat. Arrange kindling in a cone. Good for wet wood as heat rises to dry the upper sticks. 2) Log Cabin: Best for long-lasting, steady heat and cooking. Stack logs in a square. Collapses into a bed of hot coals. 3) Star Fire: Good for conserving wood. Push long logs into the center as they burn. 4) Dakota Fire Pit: A hole in the ground with an air vent. Hidden, windproof, and highly efficient.
snow_shelter:
SAS Survival Handbook — Snow Cave:
1) Find a deep snow drift at least 5ft deep. 2) Dig a tunnel into the side, then expand upward to create a chamber. 3) The floor of the chamber must be higher than the entrance tunnel (to trap rising warm air). 4) Poke a small ventilation hole through the roof with a stick. 5) Smooth the inside of the roof to prevent dripping. 6) Block the entrance with a block of snow or a pack, leaving a small air gap.
desert_shelter:
US Army FM 21-76 — Desert Survival Shelter:
1) Dig a trench 1.5ft deep and as long as your body. 2) Pile sand around the edges for extra depth. 3) Cover the trench with a double-layered roof (tarp, clothing, or branches) leaving a 4-inch gap between layers — this 'air gap' provides insulation against the sun's heat. 4) Digging down just a few inches can lower the temperature by 10-20 degrees. Stay in the shade and minimize activity during the heat of the day.
nav_skills:
US Army FM 21-76 — Dead Reckoning & Navigation:
Dead Reckoning is the process of calculating your current position by using a previously determined position and advancing that position based on known or estimated speeds over a set time and direction. 1) Pace Counting: Count every time your left foot hits the ground. 60-70 double-paces usually equals 100 meters. 2) Bearing: Always maintain a line of sight with a distant landmark (peak, odd tree) in your direction of travel to prevent 'circling.' 3) Time Estimation: Average wilderness travel speed is 2 miles per hour on flat ground, 1 mph on slopes. 4) Back-azimuth: To return, subtract 180 degrees from your current bearing.
navigation_environment:
SAS Survival Handbook — Environmental Navigation Clues:
1) Wind: Prevailing winds often sculpt trees (flagging); branches grow longer on the leeward side. 2) Sun: In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes receive more sun, making them drier and the vegetation more 'shrub-like.' 3) Water: Valleys and drainages lead to rivers. Following water downhill almost always leads to civilization, but travel can be difficult due to brush. 4) Animal Paths: Game trails often lead to water or easier passes through dense terrain. If trails converge at a 'V', you are likely heading toward water.
shadow_tip_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Shadow-Tip Method (Solar Compass):
1) Stick: Place a 3ft stick in the ground. 2) Mark 1: Mark the shadow's tip. Wait 20 mins. 3) Mark 2: Mark the new tip. 4) West-East: A line from Mark 1 to Mark 2 runs West to East. 5) North-South: Stand with the first mark (West) on your left and the second (East) on your right. You are now facing True North. 6) Precision: This method is most accurate around noon and least accurate near sunrise/sunset.
polaris_info:
NASA / US Army — Finding North (Northern Hemisphere):
1) Locate the Big Dipper (Ursa Major). 2) Find the two stars at the outer edge of the 'cup' (Dubhe and Merak). 3) Follow the line formed by these two stars outward from the cup for about five times the distance between them. 4) The bright star you reach is Polaris (the North Star). It is almost exactly over True North. The height of Polaris above the horizon is also roughly equal to your Latitude.
fracture_sprain_protocol:
Red Cross / WFA — Bone & Joint Injuries:
In the wilderness, treat all severe sprains and suspected fractures identically: stabilize and immobilize. Check CSM (Circulation, Sensation, Movement) distal to the injury before and after splinting. Re-check CSM every hour. If bone is protruding (open fracture), do not push it back in; cover with a sterile dressing and seek immediate rescue.
improvised_splinting:
Red Cross / WFA — Improvised Splinting Steps:
1) Gather Materials: Rigid supports (trekking poles, branches, backpack frames) and padding (jackets, socks, sleeping bags). 2) Position: Splint the limb exactly as it was found. Do not attempt to realign. 3) Immobilization: The splint must extend above and below the joints surrounding the injury. 4) Secure: Use belts, cloth strips, or tape. Ensure it is snug but does not cut off circulation. 5) Re-assess CSM immediately after securing.
choking_protocol:
Red Cross — Conscious Choking (5-and-5 Approach):
1) Give 5 back blows: Bend the person forward and hit them firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. 2) Give 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich): Stand behind them, wrap arms around waist, make a fist above the navel, and pull inward and upward sharply. 3) Repeat until the object is forced out or the person becomes unconscious.
drowning_cpr_protocol:
Red Cross — Drowning & CPR Basics:
1) Get the person out of the water to a firm, flat surface. 2) Check for breathing: tilt head back, lift chin, and look/listen for 10 seconds. 3) If not breathing, give 2 rescue breaths (pinch nose, seal mouth, blow until chest rises). 4) Begin chest compressions: 30 compressions (2 inches deep, 100-120 bpm) followed by 2 breaths. Continue until rescuers arrive or person breathes. Do not stop unless exhausted.
frostbite_protocol:
Red Cross — Frostbite Treatment:
Signs: white/waxy skin, numbness, hard/cold feeling. 1) Move to warm area. 2) Do not rub the area (damages tissue). 3) Soak in warm water (100-105°F / 38-40°C) until color/sensation returns. 4) Apply loose, dry dressing. 5) Place gauze between frozen fingers/toes. 6) Seek medical help immediately. Do not rewarm if there is a risk of refreezing.
tick_removal_protocol:
CDC — Tick Removal & Lyme Prevention:
1) Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible. 2) Pull upward with steady, even pressure. Don't twist or jerk the tick. 3) After removal, clean the bite area and your hands with alcohol or soap and water. 4) If you develop a rash (bullseye) or fever within several weeks, see a doctor. Do not use: nail polish, petroleum jelly, or heat to detach the tick.
vehicle_emergency_protocol:
NPS — Wilderness Vehicle Survival:
1) STAY WITH YOUR VEHICLE. It is easier for rescuers to find a car than a person. 2) Use the car as shelter from sun/cold. 3) Signal for help: Open the hood, tie a bright cloth to the antenna, and use mirrors to signal aircraft. 4) Run the engine sparingly (10 mins per hour) for heat, ensuring the exhaust pipe is clear of snow/mud. 5) If you must leave, leave a detailed note showing your direction and time of departure.
nosebleed_protocol:
Red Cross / WFA — Nosebleed (Epistaxis) Management:
1) POSITION: Sit down and tilt the head SLIGHTLY FORWARD. Do not lean back (causes blood to drain into throat/lungs). 2) PRESSURE: Firmly pinch the nostrils shut for 5-10 minutes. 3) MONITOR: Check after 10 mins; if still bleeding, repeat for 10 more mins. 4) ALTITUDE: In dry air, keep nostrils moist with saline or a thin layer of oil (jojoba/castor). 5) RESCUE: If bleeding lasts >20 mins despite pressure, or was caused by severe trauma, seek medical help.
ear_bleed_protocol:
Red Cross / WFA — Ear Bleeding & Skull Fracture:
Blood or clear fluid (CSF) draining from the ear after a head injury is a CRITICAL EMERGENCY (possible skull fracture). 1) DO NOT PACK: Do not block or plug the ear canal. 2) DRESSING: Cover the ear lightly with a sterile, dry dressing to catch flow. 3) MONITOR: Check for concussion, unequal pupils, or loss of consciousness. 4) RESCUE: Immediate evacuation is required.
heart_attack_protocol:
AHA / WFA — Chest Pain & Heart Attack:
1) STOP ACTIVITY: The patient must stop all physical exertion immediately. 2) POSITION: Sit upright in a position of comfort to ease breathing. 3) ASPIRIN: If alert and not allergic, have the patient CHEW and swallow one adult aspirin (325mg) or four baby aspirins. 4) MONITOR: Watch for loss of consciousness or cessation of breathing. 5) ARREST: If the patient becomes unresponsive and has no pulse, begin CPR immediately. 6) RESCUE: This is a high-priority medical emergency requiring rapid evacuation.
chest_pain_management:
Wilderness Medicine — Heart Attack Recognition:
Signs: 1) Chest pressure, squeezing, or pain that may spread to the jaw, neck, or left arm. 2) Shortness of breath and 'cold sweat.' 3) Nausea or lightheadedness. 4) Denial (patients often insist it is 'just indigestion'). Treat all persistent chest pain in the wilderness as a heart attack until proven otherwise.
wound_infection_watch:
WFA — Wound Infection Monitoring:
1) Signs: Increasing pain, swelling, redness, or warmth around the wound. 2) Pus: Yellow, green, or cloudy discharge. 3) Red Streaks: If you see red lines extending from the wound toward the heart, the infection is spreading to the lymphatic system (urgent medical emergency). 4) Systemic: Fever, chills, and fatigue. 5) Action: Clean the wound daily, apply local heat (if no red streaks), and keep elevated. Seek professional help if streaks or fever appear.
mental_health_management:
Red Cross / WFA — Panic & Psychological First Aid:
1) STOP: Sit down, take a breath. Panic causes fatal errors. 2) Box Breathing: Inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4. 3) Anchoring: Name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste. 4) Small Tasks: Focus on a simple, achievable goal (e.g., 'I will build a small fire'). Success builds confidence and reduces panic. 5) Keep Busy: Idle time leads to rumination. Maintain a routine.
evacuation_decision:
WFA — Evacuation Decision Tree (Stay vs. Go):
1) Stay if: You are in a safe location, you have shelter/water, rescuers are expected, or moving a patient will cause more harm. 2) Go (Self-Evacuate) if: Rescuers cannot find you, your location is becoming unsafe (rising water, fire), or you have the strength/knowledge to reach safety. 3) Moving Patients: Only move a patient with a stable spine. Use a litter or shoulder carry. Monitor CSM (Circulation, Sensation, Movement) constantly. If the situation is not deteriorating, staying put is statistically safer.
diabetic_emergency_protocol:
Red Cross / WFA — Diabetic Emergency (General Rule):
When in doubt (if no glucometer is available), ALWAYS GIVE SUGAR. Providing sugar to someone with high blood sugar will not cause immediate harm, but failing to treat low blood sugar can be rapidly fatal. Treat any altered mental status in a known diabetic as hypoglycemia first.
hypoglycemia_management:
Red Cross / ADA — Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia):
Signs: Confusion, shakiness, sweating, rapid heartbeat, cold/clammy skin. 1) CONSCIOUS: Give 15-20g of fast-acting sugar (glucose tabs, honey, candy, juice). Wait 15 mins; repeat if no improvement. 2) STABILIZE: Once alert, give a complex carb/protein snack. 3) UNCONSCIOUS: Place in recovery position. Do not put anything in the mouth. Seek immediate rescue.
hyperglycemia_management:
Red Cross / ADA — High Blood Sugar (Hyperglycemia):
Signs: Extreme thirst, fruity-smelling breath, frequent urination, dry/warm skin, nausea. 1) HYDRATE: Encourage drinking large amounts of water. 2) MEDS: Do not administer insulin for the patient; allow them to self-administer if alert. 3) RESCUE: Seek evacuation if persistent vomiting occurs or if mental status deteriorates (signs of Ketoacidosis).
seizure_protocol:
Red Cross / Epilepsy Foundation — Seizure First Aid:
1) SAFETY: Clear the area of hard/sharp objects. Place a soft object under the head. 2) DO NOT RESTRAIN: Allow the movements to happen. 3) NOTHING IN MOUTH: Do not put any objects in the mouth. 4) POSITION: Gently roll the person onto their side (Recovery Position) to keep the airway clear. 5) TIME: Note the exact start time of the seizure.
post_ictal_monitoring:
Wilderness Medicine — Recovery Phase:
After the seizure stops, the patient enters the 'post-ictal' phase, often marked by confusion and fatigue. 1) AIRWAY: Keep them on their side and monitor breathing. 2) REASSURE: Speak calmly. 3) NO FOOD/DRINK: Do not provide anything by mouth until they are fully alert and can swallow safely. 4) ASSESSMENT: Gradually assess their orientation (Who/Where/What).
seizure_rescue_criteria:
Red Cross / WFA — Seizure Emergency (When to Evacuate):
Seek immediate medical help/rescue if: 1) The seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes. 2) Multiple seizures occur without regaining consciousness. 3) The person does not wake up after the seizure. 4) An injury occurred during the fall. 5) It is their first-ever seizure. 6) The seizure occurred in water. 7) The person is pregnant or diabetic.
rope_knot_skills:
SAS Survival Handbook — Essential Survival Knots:
1) Reef Knot (Square Knot): Best for joining two ropes of equal thickness and tying bandages. 2) Bowline: Creates a fixed, non-slip loop; the 'King of Knots' for rescue and anchors. 3) Clove Hitch: Quick way to secure rope to a post or tree; starting point for most lashings. 4) Sheet Bend: Use for joining ropes of different thicknesses. 5) Taut-Line Hitch: Adjustable knot for vary tension (ideal for tent lines). 6) Round Turn & Two Half Hitches: Extremely secure for heavy loads on a tree/spar.
improvised_cordage:
SAS Survival Handbook — Making Natural Cordage:
1) Materials: Inner bark (Cedar, Willow, Elm) or fibrous stalks (Milkweed, Nettle, Yucca leaves). 2) Reverse Wrap Technique: Twist two bundles of fiber away from you, then wrap them over each other toward you. 3) Splicing: Add new fibers into the ends of existing strands as you twist to create an infinite length of strong, two-ply cordage.
signaling_improvisation:
NASAR / SAS — Visual Signal Improvisation:
1) Rule of Three: Any signal repeated 3 times is an international distress call. 2) Mirror Alternatives: Use a polished tin can bottom, belt buckle, or smartphone screen. Polish metal with fine sand or ash to increase reflectivity. 3) Aiming: Hold the object near your eye and direct the flash onto your outstretched finger, then align the finger with the target (aircraft/rescuer).
ground_to_air_codes:
NASAR — Ground-to-Air Signal Codes:
1) V: Requires Assistance. 2) X: Requires Medical Assistance. 3) Arrow: Direction of travel. 4) SOS: Save Our Souls. 5) Construction: Make symbols at least 20 feet long. Use materials that contrast sharply with the ground (e.g., dark logs on snow, light rocks on dirt).
whistle_alternatives:
SAS Survival Handbook — Audible Signal Improvisation:
1) Acorn Cap: Hold an acorn cap between your knuckles to create a high-pitched whistle. 2) Bottle Cap: A plastic bottle cap held against the lips can produce a similar piercing sound. 3) Percussion: Bang rocks together or strike metal pots/pans with a sturdy stick. Sound travels farther at dawn and dusk.
bear_encounter_protocol:
NPS / Parks Canada — Bear Safety:
1) VISUAL: Stay calm, talk firmly, and back away slowly. DO NOT RUN. 2) DEFENSIVE ATTACK (Surprise/Cubs): PLAY DEAD. Lie flat on your stomach, clasp hands behind neck, and keep your pack on. 3) PREDATORY ATTACK (Stalking/Night): DO NOT PLAY DEAD. Fight back with everything available (bear spray, rocks, sticks). Aim for the face.
wolf_encounter_protocol:
NPS / Parks Canada — Wolf Safety:
1) STANCE: Stand your ground. Do not run or crouch. 2) APPEARANCE: Look large, yell, and wave arms. Gather group/children. 3) DETERRENT: Use bear spray or throw rocks/sticks if the wolf approaches. 4) ATTACK: If bitten, fight back aggressively. Aim for eyes and nose.
boar_encounter_protocol:
Wilderness Medicine — Wild Boar Safety:
1) AVOIDANCE: Boars are highly territorial. If you see piglets, leave the area immediately. 2) ESCAPE: Climb a tree (at least 6 feet high) if a boar charges. 3) STANCE: If no tree is available, stand your ground and use a walking stick or bear spray. 4) DO NOT RUN in a straight line; boars are fast but struggle with sharp turns.
river_crossing_protocol:
US Army / WFA — River Crossing Safety:
1) ASSESSMENT: Crossing is a last resort. Choose wide, shallow, slow sections. Early morning is best for snow-melt rivers. 2) PREPARATION: Unbuckle pack straps (waist/chest) to allow rapid jettison. Keep boots ON. 3) TECHNIQUE: Use a pole for a third point of contact. Face upstream, lean into current, and shuffle sideways. 4) GROUP: Link arms for mutual support.
water_rescue_swimming:
US Army / WFA — Defensive Swimming (Swept Away):
If you lose your footing: 1) DITCH PACK immediately. 2) POSITION: Get on your back, feet pointing downstream, knees slightly bent to fend off rocks. 3) NO STANDING: Never try to stand in swift water (Foot Entrapment risk). 4) EXIT: Once stable, swim aggressively at a 45-degree angle toward the nearest safe shore.
avalanche_survival_protocol:
AIARE / Parks Canada — Avalanche Survival (If Caught):
1) ESCAPE: Move to the side of the flow; grab a tree/boulder if possible. 2) DISCARD: Release skis/poles/heavy pack. 3) SWIMMING: Use a backstroke motion to stay near the surface. 4) AIR POCKET: As the snow slows, thrust your hands in front of your face to create a breathing cavity. 5) CHEST SPACE: Take a deep breath to expand your chest before the snow sets like concrete.
avalanche_rescue_steps:
AIARE — Companion Rescue (Speed is Life):
1) SAFETY: Ensure no secondary slide risk. 2) SEARCH: Switch ALL transceivers to 'SEARCH' mode. 3) PINPOINT: Use a probe to locate the victim (leave probe in). 4) DIGGING: Start downhill from the probe; dig a ramp toward the victim. 5) AIRWAY: Clear the victim's airway the moment they are reached. 6) CARE: Treat for hypothermia and trauma immediately.
watch_compass_method:
US Army FM 21-76 — Watch Compass Navigation:
Determine rough cardinal directions using an analog watch (or a drawn watch face). 1) NORTHERN HEMISPHERE: Point the HOUR HAND at the sun. South is exactly midway between the hour hand and the 12 o'clock marker. 2) SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE: Point the 12 O'CLOCK marker at the sun. North is exactly midway between the 12 o'clock marker and the hour hand. 3) DST ADJUSTMENT: If using Daylight Savings Time, use the 1 o'clock marker instead of 12 o'clock for the midpoint calculation.
terrain_features_guide:
US Army — Land Navigation Terrain Features (HVRSD):
1) HILL: High ground sloping down in all directions. 2) VALLEY: Level ground between higher ground; U-shaped contours point to HIGH ground. 3) RIDGE: A line of high ground with variations along the crest. 4) SADDLE: A low point between two hilltops along a ridge. 5) DEPRESSION: A low point surrounded by high ground. 6) DRAW (Re-entrant): A small valley; contours point to high ground. 7) SPUR: A sloping line of high ground extending from a ridge; contours point AWAY from high ground.
pace_counting_guide:
US Army / TC 3-25.26 — Distance Estimation:
A 'pace' is two steps (count every time your left foot touches the ground). 1) BASE: Walk 100 meters on flat terrain to find your average number (usually 60-70). 2) VARIATION: Your count will INCREASE (shorter strides) on soft sand, mud, snow, or uphill. 3) LOADS: Carrying a heavy pack will also increase your pace count.
ranger_beads_tracking:
US Army — Using Ranger Beads (Pace Beads):
1) 100m TRACKING: Slide one of the lower 9 beads down every time you complete 100 meters. 2) 1km TRACKING: After 10 beads (all lower 9 plus one reset), slide one of the upper 4 beads down to mark 1000 meters (1km). 3) RESET: Reset the lower beads and continue until the next kilometer.
tsunami_warning_signs:
NOAA — Natural Tsunami Warnings:
If you experience any of these, EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: 1) Strong or long-lasting earthquake (20+ seconds). 2) LOUD ROAR from the ocean (like a train or jet). 3) UNUSUAL OCEAN BEHAVIOR: Water retreating significantly, exposing the seafloor/reefs, or a rapidly rising flood.
nuclear_radiation_protocol:
FEMA / CDC — Nuclear/Radiation Survival:
1) GET INSIDE: Find a brick or concrete building. 2) STAY INSIDE: Move to the basement or the center of the building; stay away from outer walls and roof. 2) SEAL: Turn off fans/AC and close all windows/dampers. 3) STAY TUNED: Listen to radio/official alerts and stay inside for at least 24 hours unless told otherwise. 4) KI: Do NOT take Potassium Iodide unless specifically instructed by officials.
radiation_decontamination:
CDC — Radiation Decontamination Steps:
1) CLOTHING: Gently remove outer layers; this removes ~90% of radioactive material. Seal clothes in a plastic bag. 2) WASH: Shower with soap and water (no scrubbing) or wipe exposed skin with a damp cloth. 3) HAIR: Wash hair with shampoo but avoid conditioner (it can bind radioactive dust to hair).
civil_unrest_protocol:
Red Cross / State Dept — Civil Unrest Survival:
1) SHELTER: Generally safer to stay indoors. Move away from windows and doors. Limit visibility from the street. 2) CROWDS: If caught in a crowd, move perpendicular to the flow to exit. Seek the nearest secure building. 3) VEHICLE: Stay inside with doors locked. Do not drive through crowds. 4) LAW ENFORCEMENT: Keep hands visible and follow all instructions immediately.
urban_emergency_safety:
Urban Survival — Key Safety Rules:
1) VISIBILITY: Keep a low profile. Avoid wearing high-visibility clothing or carrying expensive gear. 2) COMMUNICATION: Establish out-of-area contacts and meeting points. 3) ESCAPE: Know at least two exit routes from your neighborhood. 4) SUPPLIES: Maintain a 72-hour 'Go-Bag' with cash, documents, and essential meds.
lightning_survival_protocol:
NWS / NOAA — Lightning Safety:
1) RULE: 'When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!' If you hear thunder, you are at risk. 2) SHELTER: Seek a fully enclosed building or a hard-topped metal vehicle. Tents and open sheds provide NO protection. 3) 30-MINUTE RULE: Wait at least 30 minutes after the last sound of thunder before resuming outdoor activities. 4) AVOID: Stay away from water, tall isolated trees, and metal fences.
lightning_crouch_myth:
NWS — The Lightning Crouch Myth:
For years, squatting on the balls of your feet was recommended if caught outside. However, the NWS officially stopped recommending this in 2008. It provides NO significant protection. Your ONLY priority should be moving to a substantial building or vehicle as quickly as possible.
landslide_mudslide_protocol:
USGS / Red Cross — Landslide/Mudslide Survival:
1) EVACUATE: If you are in the path of a slide, get out immediately. 2) HIGH GROUND: Move to the nearest high ground away from the flow. 3) AVOID: Stay out of low-lying areas, river valleys, and do not cross roads with flowing mud. 4) NO EARTHQUAKE DRILL: Do not 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On'; your priority is moving out of the flow path.
landslide_warning_signs:
USGS — Landslide Warning Signs:
1) SOUNDS: Increasing rumbling, trees cracking, or boulders knocking together. 2) GROUND: New cracks in soil or bulging ground at the base of a slope. 3) STRUCTURE: Doors/windows sticking or jamming; new cracks in foundations. 4) WATER: Sudden increase/decrease in stream level or water turning muddy.
hypothermia_prevention_cold:
NOLS / WFA — The C.O.L.D. Principle:
1) CLEAN: Dirt reduces insulation loft. 2) OVERHEATING: Avoid sweating; adjust layers before you get damp. 3) LOOSE: Tight clothes restrict circulation. 4) DRY: Moisture is a massive heat thief. 5) CALORIES: Eat proactively; carbohydrates provide fast fuel for shivering heat production.
layering_system_protocol:
Wilderness Medicine — Three-Layer System:
1) BASE: Wicking layer (Merino wool or synthetic). NEVER use cotton ('Cotton Kills'). 2) MID: Insulation layer (Fleece, wool, or down puffy). 3) OUTER: Protection layer (Windproof and waterproof shell). Adjust these layers dynamically based on activity level.
water_purification_detailed:
CDC / EPA — Water Purification Methods:
1) BOILING: Surest method. Bring to rolling boil for 1 min (3 mins if >6,500ft). 2) CHEMICAL: Use 8 drops of unscented bleach per gallon; wait 30 mins. 3) SODIS: Clear water in a clear plastic bottle exposed to direct sun for 6-8 hours. 4) WARNING: None of these remove fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive materials.
water_disinfection_safety:
CDC — Safe Water Rules:
1) SETTLE: If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter through a clean cloth before treatment. 2) VIRUSES: Most portable filters do NOT remove viruses; follow filtration with chemical disinfection. 3) CONTAINERS: Use only clean, food-grade containers for storage.
wound_infection_monitoring:
Red Cross / WFA — S.H.A.R.P. Signs:
Monitor wounds for 1) SWELLING. 2) HEAT (warmth around wound). 3) ACHES (increasing pain). 4) REDNESS (spreading). 5) PUS (yellow/green discharge). SERIOUS: Red streaks radiating toward the heart, fever, or chills indicate systemic infection; evacuate immediately.
infection_treatment_wfa:
WFA — Infected Wound Treatment:
1) RE-CLEAN: High-pressure irrigation with potable water. 2) DRAINAGE: Apply warm compresses (20-30 mins, 3x daily) to draw out pus. 3) TRACK: Circle the redness with a pen to monitor spreading. 4) EVACUATE: If no improvement in 24 hours or systemic symptoms (fever) appear.
patient_monitoring_vitals:
WFA — Vital Signs Monitoring:
Record vitals every 15 mins (unstable) or 60 mins (stable). 1) PULSE: Rate (60-100 bpm), Rhythm, and Quality. 2) RESPIRATION: Rate (12-20 bpm) and Quality. 3) SKIN (CTM): Color, Temperature, and Moisture (e.g., Pale, Warm, Dry). 4) TRENDS: Document all changes to see if the patient is improving or worsening.
avpu_responsiveness_scale:
WFA — AVPU Scale (Consciousness):
1) ALERT: Fully awake and coherent. 2) VOICE: Responds only when spoken to. 3) PAIN: Responds only to painful stimulus (e.g., pinch). 4) UNRESPONSIVE: No response to any stimulus. Significant changes in AVPU require immediate rescue/evacuation.
evacuation_decision_logic:
NOLS — Evacuation Decision Tree:
1) SELF-EVACUATE: Patient can walk out; group carries their gear. 2) ASSISTED: Patient needs help walking. 3) LITTER CARRY: Patient is immobile; extremely labor-intensive and high-risk for the group. 4) WAIT: If terrain/weather makes travel lethal for the group, stay put and signal for help.
evacuation_vs_wait:
WFA — When to Evacuate Immediately:
1) LIFE/LIMB THREAT: Severe bleeding, shock, or airway issues. 2) DETERIORATION: Patient’s mental status (AVPU) or vitals are worsening. 3) INCAPACITY: The injury cannot be managed in the field. 4) RULE: Never attempt an evacuation that exceeds your group's physical capacity or endangers others.
stop_protocol:
Psychology of Survival — S.T.O.P. Rule:
1) STOP: Sit down and stop moving to interrupt panic. 2) THINK: Take a breath and acknowledge the situation calmly. 3) OBSERVE: Assess your environment, gear, and physical condition. 4) PLAN: Break large problems into small, manageable tasks.
box_breathing_technique:
Tactical Breathing — Box Breathing:
Use this to lower heart rate and regain focus: 1) INHALE slowly for 4 seconds. 2) HOLD for 4 seconds. 3) EXHALE slowly for 4 seconds. 4) HOLD for 4 seconds. Repeat for several minutes until calm.
stroke_protocol:
CDC / American Stroke Association - Stroke Recognition:
During a stroke, every minute counts. Use FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech trouble, Time to call emergency services. Also watch for sudden confusion, vision trouble, dizziness/loss of balance, or severe unexplained headache. Note the exact time symptoms started or when the person was last known well. Do not give food, drink, or aspirin unless a clinician directs it.
stroke_fast_check:
CDC - FAST Field Check:
Ask the person to smile, raise both arms, and repeat a simple sentence. Any new one-sided face droop, arm drift/weakness, slurred speech, confusion, or trouble understanding speech is an emergency. Keep the person at rest, monitor breathing, and prepare a medication/allergy list for responders.
asthma_breathing_protocol:
Red Cross / CDC - Asthma or Severe Breathing Difficulty:
Help the person sit upright and stay calm. Assist with their prescribed quick-relief inhaler if available. Call emergency services if they cannot speak more than a few words, lips/fingernails look blue or gray, breathing is very rapid or shallow, symptoms do not improve after medication, or the person becomes drowsy/confused.
asthma_inhaler_steps:
Red Cross - Quick-Relief Inhaler Support:
Verify the medication belongs to the person. Shake the inhaler, attach a spacer if available, have them breathe out, seal lips around the mouthpiece, press once, and have them breathe in slowly then hold for 5-10 seconds if able. If using a spacer and they cannot take a deep breath, have them take several normal breaths. Note time and response.
opioid_overdose_protocol:
SAMHSA - Suspected Opioid Overdose:
Opioid overdose is life-threatening. Signs include very slow or stopped breathing, blue/gray lips or fingernails, gurgling/snoring sounds, limp body, pale clammy skin, vomiting, or inability to wake/speak. Call emergency services immediately. Give naloxone/nalmefene if available and begin CPR if breathing stops or is only gasping.
naloxone_steps:
SAMHSA / FDA - Naloxone Field Use:
Give naloxone exactly as labeled, usually nasal spray into one nostril or injection if trained. Naloxone is temporary and may wear off before opioids do, so medical care is still urgent. Keep monitoring breathing. If breathing improves, place the person in recovery position. If breathing does not improve, continue CPR if trained and follow the product directions for repeat dosing.
pregnancy_labor_protocol:
CDC / Red Cross - Pregnancy and Labor Emergency:
Call emergency services for heavy vaginal bleeding, seizure, fainting, severe abdominal pain, trouble breathing, severe headache/vision changes, signs of shock, or birth that seems imminent without medical help. Keep the parent warm, private, and as clean as possible. Do not give food or drink if surgery or urgent transport may be needed.
imminent_birth_steps:
Red Cross / WHO - Imminent Birth Field Support:
Wash hands or use gloves if available. Let birth happen naturally; do not pull on the baby or cord. Support the head and body as they deliver, keep the baby level with the parent, dry and warm the baby immediately, and keep skin-to-skin if breathing well. Do not cut the cord unless trained and equipped. Watch the parent for heavy bleeding.
newborn_immediate_care:
WHO / Red Cross - Newborn First Minutes:
Dry the baby thoroughly, keep warm skin-to-skin, cover the head, and check breathing/crying. If the baby is not breathing, stimulate by rubbing the back or feet and seek emergency help immediately. Keep the baby and parent warm together and monitor for heavy bleeding, weak breathing, blue color, or poor responsiveness.
mental_health_crisis_protocol:
NIMH / 988 Lifeline - Suicide or Mental Health Crisis:
Warning signs include talking about wanting to die, feeling trapped or unbearable pain, making a plan, giving away possessions, extreme agitation, or increased substance use. If there is immediate danger, call emergency services. In the U.S., call or text 988. Stay with the person, listen without judgment, and move weapons, pills, or other lethal means away only if safe.
mental_health_stabilize:
NIMH / 988 Lifeline - Crisis Stabilization:
Use calm, direct language. Ask clearly if they are thinking about killing themselves; asking does not put the idea in their head. Do not leave them alone if risk is present. Reduce stimulation, avoid arguing, connect them with a crisis line or trusted person, and document location and immediate hazards for responders.
mass_casualty_triage:
FEMA / START Triage - Multiple Injured People:
Scene safety comes first. Call for help early and give location, hazards, and number injured. Ask anyone who can walk to move to a safe area. Prioritize people who cannot walk, are not breathing normally, have severe bleeding, or are confused/unable to follow commands. Control catastrophic bleeding, open airways, and use bystanders for simple tasks.
power_outage_protocol:
Ready.gov / CDC - Power Outage Safety:
Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed. Use flashlights instead of candles when possible. Disconnect sensitive electronics to prevent surge damage. Use generators, grills, and camp stoves only outdoors and away from windows; never use a gas stove or oven to heat the home. Plan backup power or relocation for power-dependent medical devices.
power_medical_device_plan:
Ready.gov - Power-Dependent Medical Equipment:
Conserve device battery, switch to backup power if available, notify emergency services or utility support if a medical device depends on electricity, and move to a powered shelter or medical facility if power will not return in time. Keep medicines cool only as directed and seek pharmacist/clinician guidance for refrigerated medications exposed to heat.
gas_co_triage:
CDC / Ready.gov - Gas and Carbon Monoxide Triage:
Carbon monoxide cannot be seen or smelled. Suspect CO when several people have headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, confusion, or collapse near generators, vehicles, grills, furnaces, or fuel-burning heaters. For gas smell or hissing, treat as explosion risk and leave immediately.
carbon_monoxide_protocol:
CDC - Carbon Monoxide Exposure:
Move everyone to fresh air immediately. Call emergency services or poison control. Do not re-enter the area until professionals say it is safe. If someone is unconscious or not breathing normally, start CPR if trained and keep yourself out of the contaminated area.
gas_leak_protocol:
Fire Safety / Utility Emergency Guidance - Gas Leak:
Leave immediately. Do not turn lights on or off, use phones inside, light flames, start vehicles near the leak, or operate appliances. From a safe distance outside, call emergency services or the gas utility. Keep others away from the area until professionals clear it.
chemical_spill_protocol:
CDC / FEMA - Chemical Spill or Release:
Move away from the source. Outdoors, go uphill and upwind when possible. Avoid vapors, liquids, powders, and contaminated surfaces. Remove contaminated clothing if safe and rinse exposed skin or eyes with clean water. Bring chemical labels or photos only if it can be done without exposure. Seek emergency help for breathing trouble, burns, eye exposure, or altered mental status.
infectious_disease_protocol:
CDC / WHO - Infectious Disease Isolation During Emergencies:
Separate the sick person if possible, improve ventilation, use masks when available, wash hands, avoid sharing cups/utensils, clean high-touch surfaces, and protect high-risk people. Seek urgent help for trouble breathing, blue lips, confusion, dehydration, severe weakness, chest pain, or worsening condition.
infection_control_steps:
CDC / WHO - Household Infection Control:
Use one caregiver if possible, keep the sick person in a separate area, clean hands before and after contact, handle laundry carefully, disinfect high-touch surfaces, and monitor temperature, breathing, hydration, and mental status. Keep a written timeline of symptoms and exposures for clinicians.
